title: Net-Zero Pace
scope: How fast rich economies should decarbonize. Pace and cost, not whether growth must stop.
primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: A suburban house sits on a curved green hill as the dominant mass, its roof covered in solar panels, a heat pump unit beside its wall and an electric car parked at a small charger in front, the car overlapping the house corner. Behind the house on a farther hill stand a medium factory chimney with a soft pale plume and two small wind turbines. Power lines run from the distant hill across the whole frame down to the house.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3f9a6a, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: clocks, hourglasses, countdown timers, calendars, the numbers 2050 or any year, thermometers, flames, burning or melting globes, dollar signs or coins, up or down arrows, finish lines or flags, checkered flags, speedometers, traffic lights, stop signs, dark smoke, smog, dead trees, cracked earth, a balance scale, a split or mirrored composition

overview.summary: Most rich economies aim for net zero, mostly by 2050. The central argument is whether faster cuts are worth the cost, with fairness and backlash close behind.
overview.scope_covered: How fast high-income economies should cut emissions: interim targets, the costs to households, budgets and industry, who pays, and the effect on other countries.
overview.scope_excluded: Whether economic growth must stop, the design of carbon prices, restricting fossil fuel extraction, and carbon removal, except where they change the pace argument.
overview.why_now: The UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, closed on November 22, 2026, nearly 50 hours late, after at least 32 countries rejected its cover decision; the EU said it would not endorse a text that “does not even mention fossil fuels.”

stats.label: Average annual cut in fossil CO2, 2015–2025
stats.note: Calculated from Our World in Data’s totals, high-income countries cut fossil CO2 by about 0.9 percent a year over 2015–2025; the UK, EU and Japan by about 2.5.
stats.detail: These are compound averages worked out from the dataset’s annual totals for 2015 and 2025, not rates Our World in Data publishes itself. The UK fell from 422 to 320 million tonnes, the EU from 3,083 to 2,405, Japan from 1,218 to 960, the United States from 5,366 to 5,036, and high-income countries as a group from 15,169 to 13,871. The figures count territorial emissions from fossil fuels and industry and leave out land use. For comparison, UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026 puts the global cut needed on its lowest-overshoot 1.5 °C path at about 5.7 percent a year over the next decade.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, CO2 and greenhouse gas emissions (Global Carbon Project data)

stats.label: Remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C, 50 percent chance
stats.note: The Global Carbon Project puts the CO2 that can still be emitted for even odds of holding 1.5 °C at 150 billion tonnes from 2027, less than four years of current emissions.
stats.detail: A carbon budget is the total CO2 that can still be emitted for a stated chance of holding a stated temperature. It shrinks each year by that year’s emissions, 43.3 billion tonnes in 2026 including land use, and is revised as the science improves: a year earlier the Global Carbon Project put it at 170 billion tonnes from January 2026. Carbon Brief’s analysis of the 2026 release gives the matching budgets for 1.7 °C and 2 °C as 510 and 1,035 billion tonnes. A budget this small is why UNEP and the Global Carbon Project now speak of overshooting 1.5 °C and coming back down, and why much of the argument has moved to how much extra warming each year of emissions buys.
stats.source_label: Global Carbon Budget 2026, University of Exeter release

stats.label: Net cost of UK net zero, Climate Change Committee pathway
stats.note: The Climate Change Committee puts the net cost of the UK’s path at about 0.2 percent of GDP a year; the government’s 2026 assessment puts net investment costs at about 1.2 percent.
stats.detail: Both are net figures: upfront spending on heat pumps, grids, electric vehicles and industry, minus the fuel and running-cost savings that follow. The committee expects net savings to begin within the 2038–42 budget period, and says household savings on driving roughly match any extra home-energy costs, provided policy costs come off electricity bills. The government’s impact assessment, reported by Carbon Brief in June 2026, gives a range of 0.8 to 1.6 percent because it assumes less behavior change and slower falls in technology costs, and it still finds net benefits of £865 billion against a no-net-zero scenario, most of them avoided climate damage. The Conservative Party and the think tank Onward argue that the system costs of a clean grid are higher than either assumes; climate campaigners argue that the damage avoided is understated.
stats.source_label: Climate Change Committee, The Seventh Carbon Budget

stats.label: EU net emissions cut since 1990, achieved and targeted
stats.note: The European Environment Agency puts EU net emissions 39 percent below 1990 in 2025; with planned measures they reach 54 percent by 2030, just short of the 55 percent target.
stats.detail: The 2025 figure is preliminary. EU net emissions fell 1.6 percent that year, and the agency found the pace of cuts slowing. Getting from 39 to 55 percent in five years works out to about 5.9 percent a year. The agency said cuts in buildings, road transport, agriculture and small industry over the next five years would have to match those of the previous two decades combined. Those who defend the targets note that the cheapest cuts, in power, are done and that the next ones depend on a turnover of boilers and cars already under way; those who want the targets eased read the same arithmetic as proof the dates are unrealistic.
stats.source_label: European Environment Agency, Trends and projections in Europe 2026

stats.label: High-income countries’ share of fossil CO2 since 1750
stats.note: Our World in Data’s figures put high-income countries at about 62 percent of all fossil CO2 emitted since 1750, and about 36 percent of the 2025 total.
stats.detail: Cumulative emissions matter because warming tracks the total CO2 ever emitted rather than any one year’s output. On the same basis the United States accounts for 23 percent of the cumulative total, the EU and China 16 percent each, the UK 4.3 percent, India 3.7 percent and all low-income countries together 0.6 percent. The figures exclude land-use change; counting deforestation would raise the historical shares of countries such as Brazil and Indonesia. Those who argue that rich countries owe a faster pace start from the cumulative figure; those who argue for a shared timetable point to China’s total now matching the EU’s.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, share of cumulative CO2 (Global Carbon Project data)

stats.label: Projected warming by 2100
stats.note: UNEP projects about 2.8 °C of warming by 2100 under current policies; meeting every pledge and net-zero target would hold it to about 2.1 °C.
stats.detail: Each figure is the warming with a 66 percent chance of not being exceeded, for policies as of September 1, 2026. UNEP attributes the worsening since its 2025 report mainly to the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and to revised historical emissions data. The gap between 2.6 and 2.1 °C is what net-zero targets are worth if they are kept, which is why the credibility of rich-country net-zero dates bears on the global number. UNEP found most G20 members’ trajectories misaligned with their own net-zero targets, and that every G20 member except Japan, the EU and the UK would need to cut faster than current policies imply to meet them. It also estimated that each five years of delay in starting cuts locks in about another 0.1 °C.
stats.source_label: UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026, as reported by Carbon Brief

stats.label: Required UK cuts to 2030 backed by credible plans
stats.note: The Climate Change Committee judged in June 2026 that credible policies cover 44 percent of the cuts the UK needs for its 2030 target, and that 17 percent are covered by no policy.
stats.detail: The 2030 target is 68 percent below 1990. Of the rest of the required cuts, the committee rated 15 percent as backed by plans with some risks, 19 percent by plans with significant risks and 4 percent by insufficient plans. Counting credible and partly risky plans together, emissions would reach 356 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2030 against the 291 required. The committee also found the UK highly likely to meet its fourth carbon budget, for 2023–27, with 2025 emissions 11 percent below the required annual average. Beyond 2030, the UK’s pledge under the Paris Agreement is a cut of at least 81 percent by 2035.
stats.source_label: Climate Change Committee, Progress in reducing emissions: 2026 report to Parliament

stats.label: Cost of net zero to UK public finances, to 2050–51
stats.note: The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates net zero will cost UK public finances £803 billion to 2050–51, about two-thirds of it lost fuel duty.
stats.detail: That is about 21 percent of 2025 GDP, roughly £30 billion a year, and 9 percent of GDP less than the OBR’s 2021 estimate because clean technology has become cheaper. In a long-horizon scenario of about 3 °C of global warming, the OBR finds climate change adding about 74 percent of GDP to government debt by the early 2070s, around three-fifths of it from damage and around a tenth from mitigation. It calls that a scenario with high uncertainty, not a forecast, and stresses that damage costs depend on what the big global emitters do rather than on UK policy alone, which is the hinge of the argument over how fast one country should go.
stats.source_label: Office for Budget Responsibility, Fiscal risks and sustainability, July 2025

stats.label: Estimates of the social cost of carbon
stats.note: Rennert and colleagues put the damage from one more tonne of CO2 at $185; other estimates run from about $66 to more than $1,200, on different methods, price years and discount rates.
stats.detail: The social cost of carbon is the present value of the future damage done by emitting one extra tonne today. In cost-benefit terms a high value supports fast cuts even at a high cost per tonne, and a low one a gradual path. Rennert et al. (Nature, 2022) give $185 in 2020 dollars at a 2 percent discount rate, with a range of $44 to $413, 3.6 times the $51 federal interim value then in use. Barrage and Nordhaus (PNAS, 2024) get $66 for 2020, in 2019 dollars, with the DICE-2023 model. Bilal and Känzig (NBER working paper) estimate that 1 °C of global warming cuts world GDP by over 20 percent in the long run, implying more than $1,200. A widely cited 2024 Nature paper by Kotz, Levermann and Wenz projecting a 19 percent income loss by 2049 was retracted in December 2025 after data errors were found; its authors say a corrected analysis gives about 17 percent (Retraction Watch, 2025).
stats.source_label: Resources for the Future, on Rennert et al. (2022); other rows from the studies named

stats.label: Warming by 2100 on the DICE-2023 cost-benefit optimal path
stats.note: In the DICE-2023 model, the path that best balances the cost of cutting against the damage avoided warms the world about 2.6 °C by 2100.
stats.detail: DICE, built by the Nobel laureate William Nordhaus, is the reference model for pacing climate policy by weighing costs against benefits rather than by a temperature target. Measured against a baseline path, Barrage and Nordhaus put the present-value gain at about $120 trillion on the optimal path, $107 trillion on a path limited to 2 °C and $85 trillion on an extended Paris path, in 2019 international dollars. The 2023 revision moved the optimum markedly lower than earlier versions and found 2 °C cheaper to reach. Critics, including the authors of the newer damage studies, argue its damage function is far too mild; its defenders say it is the most transparent model available and that its answer now sits between 2 and 3 °C.
stats.source_label: Barrage & Nordhaus, Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model, PNAS

stats.label: Global cut needed on the lowest-overshoot 1.5 °C path
stats.note: UNEP finds global emissions must fall 45 percent below 2025 levels by 2035 to return to 1.5 °C after the smallest overshoot; full delivery of current pledges gives 11 to 15 percent.
stats.detail: The path peaks at around 1.7 to 1.8 °C near mid-century and needs net-zero CO2 around 2050. For a path below 2 °C the cuts are 11 percent by 2030, 24 by 2035 and 37 by 2040; current pledges, fully delivered, give 5 to 8 percent by 2030. UNEP rebased its benchmarks on 2025 because the older IPCC figures, 43 percent by 2030 and 60 percent by 2035 relative to 2019, can no longer be met. These are global numbers. Most equity frameworks, and the IEA’s net-zero pathway, ask rich economies to cut faster than the average so that developing economies can cut more slowly.
stats.source_label: UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026, as reported by Carbon Brief

stats.label: IEA net-zero pathway, cut in energy CO2 by 2035
stats.note: The IEA’s net-zero pathway has advanced economies cutting energy-sector CO2 80 percent below 2022 levels by 2035 and reaching net zero around 2045 in aggregate.
stats.detail: On the same pathway, emerging market and developing economies cut 60 percent by 2035, China reaches net zero around 2050 and other developing economies after 2050, so the rich economies finish about five years ahead of the world. The IEA called on almost all countries to bring their net-zero dates forward as part of what it described as an equitable path. The pathway dates from 2023 and is built around a 1.5 °C goal that UNEP judged in 2026 can no longer be met without overshoot.
stats.source_label: IEA, Net Zero Roadmap: A Global Pathway to Keep the 1.5 °C Goal in Reach, 2023 update

stats.label: Fossil CO2 per person, 2025
stats.note: Per person, the United States emits about 14.5 tonnes of fossil CO2 a year, three times the world average of 4.7; the UK, at 4.6, is now just below it.
stats.detail: These are territorial figures, counting emissions where they are produced; Australia, at 14.0 tonnes, sits beside the United States and Canada. On a consumption basis, which adds the emissions embodied in imports, the rich economies look higher: in Our World in Data’s 2024 consumption-based figures the UK is about 7.1 tonnes per person against 4.6 territorial, the EU about 7.2 against 5.4 and the US about 15.8 against 14.2, while China falls from 8.7 to 7.7. Those who doubt rich-country progress cite that gap as evidence that some cuts were offshored; others answer that UK and EU consumption emissions have fallen too.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, CO2 emissions per capita (Global Carbon Project data)

stats.label: Global average cost of new power, 2025
stats.note: IRENA puts the 2025 global average cost of new solar power at $44 per MWh and onshore wind at $33; over 90 percent of new utility-scale renewable projects undercut the cheapest new fossil option.
stats.detail: These are levelized costs, lifetime cost divided by lifetime output. After more than a decade of steep declines, IRENA reports that solar and onshore wind costs have begun to level off, while gas generation grew dearer because of a shortage of gas turbines and, in 2026, the Middle East conflict. The installed cost of four-hour utility-scale battery storage fell close to 30 percent in 2025, to around $140 per kilowatt-hour, and the best solar-plus-battery sites now deliver round-the-clock power below $85 per MWh. Levelized costs leave out grid, balancing and backup costs, which is where much of the rich-country argument over very fast power decarbonization now sits.
stats.source_label: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2025

stats.label: Global energy investment, 2026
stats.note: The IEA expects $2.2 trillion of clean energy investment in 2026, nearly twice the $1.2 trillion going to oil, gas and coal.
stats.detail: Clean energy here covers renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, low-emission fuels, efficiency and electrification, out of a total of about $3.4 trillion. Upstream oil investment was set to stay below $500 billion for a third straight annual fall. Both sides of the pace argument find support in the figures: coal supply investment reached its highest level since 2012 and gas investment its highest in a decade. IEA executive director Fatih Birol called the 2026 Hormuz disruption the largest energy security crisis the world has faced.

stats.label: Projected change in fossil CO2, 2025 to 2026
stats.note: The Global Carbon Project projects world fossil CO2 to fall 0.4 percent in 2026, to 38.2 billion tonnes, with the EU, US, Japan and China down and India up 4.4 percent.
stats.detail: The fall is mostly oil, down 1.9 percent after the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz from March 2026 cut oil use; gas fell 0.3 percent and coal rose 0.6 percent. Emissions in the rest of the world are projected to fall 0.7 percent. The lead author, Pierre Friedlingstein, said that “a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” and that further acceleration is needed for global emissions to peak and enter a sustained decline.
stats.source_label: Global Carbon Budget 2026, University of Exeter release

stats.label: Human-induced warming, 2025
stats.note: Human activity had warmed the world 1.37 °C above 1850–1900 by 2025, and that warming is rising by about 0.27 °C a decade.
stats.detail: Over the decade 2016–2025, observed warming averaged 1.26 °C, of which 1.24 °C was human-induced. At 0.27 °C a decade, human-induced warming would reach 1.5 °C within about five years. Both the UN Environment Programme and the Global Carbon Project now treat an overshoot of 1.5 °C as unavoidable. The rate of warming, and not only its level, is what a change in the pace of emissions cuts affects first.
stats.source_label: Forster et al., Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025, Earth System Science Data

stats.label: UK adults’ expected effect of net zero on the economy
stats.note: 39 percent of UK adults expect net zero to hurt the economy in the next one to two years and 22 percent expect it to help; over ten years or more, 51 percent expect help and 24 percent harm.
stats.detail: The question asked: “What impact do you think the UK’s transition to Net Zero might have on the UK economy?” Fieldwork ran from July 7 to August 12, 2026. The same wave found 79 percent of adults concerned about climate change, down from 85 percent in autumn 2021, and 91 percent aware of net zero. The share expecting long-term harm has risen from 18 percent in summer 2023. Those who want to hold or speed the path read the split as support for the destination; those who want to slow it read the short-run figure as a warning about consent.
stats.source_label: DESNZ Public Attitudes Tracker, Net zero and climate change, Summer 2026

stats.label: Electric share of new car sales, world, 2025
stats.note: About a quarter of new cars sold worldwide in 2025 were electric, more than 20 million in all; in the EU the share was just under 27 percent.
stats.detail: Road transport is now the UK’s largest-emitting sector, 31 percent of the 2025 total in the government’s provisional figures, so the speed at which car fleets turn over sets much of the rich-economy pace. Germany’s electric share was about 30 percent. The EU has moved to soften its 2035 car standard: the European Commission proposed a 90 percent fleet cut instead of 100 percent in December 2025, and on November 4, 2026 the European Parliament’s environment committee voted for an effective floor of 87.5 percent with steel credits (electrive, 2026).

questions.text: Are the damages a faster pace avoids larger than the costs it adds?
questions.why: Every pace argument ends in this comparison, and both halves are uncertain: published estimates of the harm done per tonne differ more than tenfold, and official estimates of what a single national target costs differ several-fold.
questions.detail:
The case that damages are larger rests on newer empirical work that ties losses to global rather than local temperature and captures the extremes that do the most harm, finding damage far above what older models assumed. Mitigation keeps getting cheaper, and recent revisions have moved the cost-benefit answer toward more and faster action; even the 2023 update of the best-known cost-benefit model lowered its optimal temperature. Tail risks, from tipping points to food-system shocks, are poorly priced in every model, which argues for buying insurance early.

The case that costs rival damages starts from that same model, which still puts the best path near 2.6 °C rather than 1.5 °C. Headline damage estimates have proved fragile: one was retracted in 2025, and others stretch a few decades of noisy data across centuries. Rich-country costs also include rising network charges, industrial closures and the political price of higher bills, which arrive now and with certainty, while damages arrive later and depend mostly on what the largest emitters do.

questions.text: Do rich countries owe a faster pace because of their past emissions?
questions.why: Rich countries emitted most of the fossil CO2 released since 1750 but much less of today’s. Whether that history creates a duty to move faster now is a moral question the Paris Agreement left vague under common but differentiated responsibilities.
questions.detail:
The case for a historical debt is that warming depends on cumulative emissions, so the atmospheric space rich countries used is space no one else can use. Equal-per-person or capability-based shares of the remaining budget leave wealthy nations little or none of it. Rich countries also have the capital, institutions and technology to move fastest at the lowest relative cost, and their early deployment is what made solar, wind and batteries cheap for everyone. Asking the same timetable of a country with a tenth of the income per person is not equal treatment.

The case for a shared timetable is that most historical emissions were made before the harm was known, by people now dead, while building technologies the whole world uses. Responsibility should follow present and future emissions, now dominated by middle-income economies; China emits more per person than the EU. Charging today’s rich-country households, many of them on low incomes, a premium for their great-grandparents’ coal is hard to defend and harder to sustain. The climate does not care where a tonne is cut, so the fair and efficient course is to cut where it is cheapest and help others do the same.

questions.text: Does faster rich-country action pull global emissions down, or does it leak elsewhere?
questions.why: A rich economy’s pace matters to the climate mostly through its effect on everyone else’s emissions. Clean technology got cheaper after early deployment, but heavy industry has also moved to places with cheaper energy and looser rules.
questions.detail:
The leadership case is that deployment drives learning curves, and learning curves are global: the collapse in solar costs was bought partly by early rich-country subsidies. Credible targets anchor investors, set standards that exporters must meet, as the EU’s carbon border adjustment is pulling trading partners into carbon pricing, and give negotiators standing to ask others to move. Carbon Brief’s analysis of the 2026 Global Carbon Budget counts 40 countries, with 26 percent of global fossil emissions, that cut emissions while growing their economies over 2016–2025, up from 22 in the decade before.

The leakage case is that when energy-intensive industry in Europe closes, the steel, chemicals and fertilizer are made elsewhere, often with more emissions, and workers lose jobs for no climate gain. Consumption-based accounts, which count the emissions in imports, put UK and EU footprints well above their territorial figures. And the learning curves are now driven by China’s manufacturing scale rather than Western deadlines, so a faster domestic pace buys little extra cost decline.

questions.text: Do binding legal deadlines hold the pace, or provoke the backlash that stops it?
questions.why: Climate laws in the UK and the EU were designed to take pace out of the electoral cycle. Since 2023 the deadlines themselves have become campaign targets, and several of the rules meant to meet them have been loosened.
questions.detail:
The anchoring case is that investors in grids, factories and power plants work on 20- to 40-year horizons and need rules that will not change. The UK’s framework has survived every change of government since 2008 while emissions fell and the economy grew, and business groups repeatedly say that policy reversals, not targets, raise the cost of capital. On this view backlash follows visible costs and weak delivery rather than the deadline itself, and fixing delivery, for example by moving policy costs off electricity bills, keeps support for the destination.

The backlash case is that a fixed date in law turns every missed milestone into a crisis and every cost into a mandate, an easy target for the parties promising repeal that have gained ground since 2023. Where targets are loosened in practice anyway, through car rules, delays to carbon trading or international credits, the law loses credibility while still carrying the political cost. Durable progress, on this view, comes from making clean options cheap enough that they need no deadline.

questions.text: Does a faster transition make rich economies more or less exposed to energy-price shocks?
questions.why: Two price shocks in four years, after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and after the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, made energy security the frame in which many voters meet the pace argument, and each side reads the shocks as proof.
questions.detail:
The case that faster is safer is that oil and gas are priced on world markets a single strait can close, while domestic wind, solar, nuclear and heat pumps are not. After the 2026 shock, the Climate Change Committee found bills rose almost four times as much for a UK household with a gas boiler and petrol car as for one with a heat pump and electric car, and the IEA estimated that clean energy, electrification and efficiency saved the five largest fuel-importing regions about $260 billion in import costs in 2025.

The case that faster is costlier is that a grid relying heavily on weather-dependent power needs backup, storage and transmission that headline cost figures leave out, and those costs reach households through network charges and levies on electricity bills. Closing domestic oil and gas production while still burning imported fuel worsens security, and clean-technology supply chains are concentrated, mostly in China, so a rushed transition swaps one dependency for another. The secure path, on this view, keeps firm domestic capacity while electrification moves at the speed equipment turnover allows.

questions.text: How heavily should future harms be discounted against today’s costs?
questions.why: The costs of cutting come now and most of the benefits decades later, so the discount rate largely sets the pace a cost-benefit analysis recommends. The choice mixes ethics, how much later generations count, with economics, what capital earns.
questions.detail:
The case for a low rate is that there is no ethical reason to value a child born in 2070 less than one born today simply because of the date. The pure rate of time preference should be near zero, as Frank Ramsey and Nicholas Stern argued, leaving only an allowance for future people being richer. Climate damage may be large, irreversible and concentrated on poorer people rather than a small loss that growth will cover. The 2023 US government update and the Rennert estimate both moved to about 2 percent.

The case for a market rate is that money spent cutting emissions today is money not invested in schools, health and infrastructure that would leave future generations richer and more resilient. The rate should reflect the real returns those alternatives earn, as William Nordhaus has long argued; setting it near zero makes almost any present sacrifice look worthwhile and is a value choice dressed as arithmetic. Future people will very likely be richer and better equipped, so heavy spending by today’s households on their behalf is a transfer from poorer to richer.

questions.text: If 1.5 °C can no longer be met without overshoot, should it still set the rich-country pace?
questions.why: Overshooting a goal changes what the goal can mean. Whether it makes speed more urgent or makes the timetables built for 1.5 °C obsolete is a judgment about what a climate target is for.
questions.detail:
The case for keeping 1.5 °C as the compass is that every tenth of a degree matters to damages, and the lowest-overshoot path still caps the peak at around 1.7 to 1.8 °C and brings warming back toward 1.5 °C by 2100; dropping the goal would remove the main argument for that path. The Paris temperature goal is a legal commitment, which the International Court of Justice’s 2025 advisory opinion treated as the standard for judging state conduct. Overshoot makes speed more important, because every year above the line must later be paid back with costly removals.

The case for resetting is that a target that cannot be met stops guiding behavior and becomes a reason to distrust every target. Timetables built on budgets that are now gone yield dates for rich countries, net zero by 2035 or 2040, that are impossible without economic disruption voters will not accept. A realistic goal, such as holding warming well below 2 °C with more emphasis on adaptation and resilience, would let governments set credible paths and measure progress by human welfare rather than temperature.

questions.text: Should rich countries count international credits and removals toward their targets?
questions.why: The EU’s 2040 target lets up to 5 of its 90 percentage points come from international credits from 2036. Its scientific advisory board warned this could weaken domestic cuts; supporters say it buys the same climate outcome for less.
questions.detail:
The case for domestic cuts only is that rich countries are the ones with the money to transform their own economies, and every tonne bought abroad is domestic change postponed. The history of carbon offsets is full of credits that did not represent real cuts. Every country must reach net zero eventually, so a cheap cut bought in a developing economy is one that country can no longer count toward its own target, and domestic transformation builds the industries and supply chains that are the real prize of the transition.

The case for cutting where it is cheapest is that the atmosphere does not care where a tonne is avoided, and the same money buys several times more abatement in a coal-heavy developing economy than on an already clean European grid. High-integrity credits under the Paris Agreement’s Article 6 rules move finance to where it is most needed and let rich countries keep ambitious targets without forcing the steepest, costliest last cuts at home. Removals are not a loophole but the only answer to residual emissions in farming, aviation and cement.

positions.name: Hold the 2050 course with steep cuts this decade
positions.steelman: Net zero by 2050, with the deepest cuts front-loaded, is the pace the science sets and the economics now supports; the job now is delivery, not renegotiation.
positions.detail:
The cheap phase is under way. Renewables undercut new fossil power in most markets, electric cars are a quarter of global sales, and heat pumps and electric cars already give households lower and steadier bills than gas and petrol. Legislated dates give investors the certainty to build grids, factories and power plants on 30-year horizons, and interim budgets keep the path honest: under its framework the UK cut emissions 54 percent below 1990 by 2025 while its economy grew. The UK’s statutory adviser reckons the whole transition costs, net, around 0.2 percent of national output each year, turning to net savings by the 2038–42 budget period. As UK Energy Secretary Ed Miliband put it in 2026, “the only way to protect family and business finances is to drive for clean homegrown power that we control.”

Slipping milestones are a delivery problem with known fixes: move levies off electricity bills, connect grids and approve projects faster, and support low-income households. A missed milestone is a reason to strengthen policy, not to move the goalposts, because every delay means steeper, costlier cuts later and more warming locked in. Going slower would leave rich economies exposed to the next oil and gas shock and hand this century’s clean industries to China. Those demanding faster cuts are right about the science but wrong about what voters and supply chains can absorb in the 2020s; those demanding repeal would trade a manageable cost for lasting exposure to fossil price shocks.
positions.proponents: UK Government; Ed Miliband; Government of Japan

positions.name: Keep net zero but ease near-term mandates
positions.steelman: Keep the 2050 goal in law, but give households and industry more time and flexibility on the route; easing the near term is what saves the long term.
positions.detail:
The destination is right, but the near-term schedule was set when energy was cheap and before two price shocks, and it now asks households and industry to move faster than technology, supply chains and incomes allow. Forcing people to replace boilers and cars on a fixed date, or loading carbon costs onto heating and fuel bills in a cost-of-living crisis, risks the public consent the 2050 target depends on. Keep the long-term goal and the carbon price, and allow flexibility on the route: technology neutrality, international credits, phased mandates and more time for the hardest sectors. Rishi Sunak eased the UK’s car and boiler rules in 2023 for what he called “a more pragmatic, proportionate, and realistic approach to meeting Net Zero”; France and Germany proposed in October 2026 a 90 percent rather than a 100 percent car CO2 cut for 2035.

The delivery gap is our evidence: credible UK policy covers less than half the cuts needed for 2030, and the EU is projected to fall short of its own 2030 goal even with planned measures. Emissions trading does far more for the climate than car rules, so easing a mandate costs little in emissions. A target that is visibly unrealistic damages investment certainty more than an honest adjustment does, and a target repealed by a backlash government damages it most of all. To those who would repeal, we say the cuts already made show the goal is affordable when the route is flexible; to those who want faster cuts, that consent is the binding constraint, and ignoring it is how targets get lost altogether.
positions.proponents: European People’s Party Group; Rishi Sunak; Government of France; Government of Germany; Conservative Environment Network

positions.name: Repeal binding net-zero targets
positions.steelman: Binding deadlines force decarbonization at any price; aim energy policy at cheap, secure power, and emissions will keep falling wherever clean options are genuinely cheaper.
positions.detail:
Deadlines set in law decades ahead force governments to buy decarbonization at any price, and the price is landing on households and industry as some of the highest electricity costs in the developed world, closed factories and lost jobs, while emissions move to China and India. A country with about 1 percent of global fossil CO2 cannot change the climate by going faster than everyone else; it can only make itself poorer and less secure. The UK and EU together emit about 7 percent, India’s emissions are projected to rise 4.4 percent in 2026 alone, and COP31 ended without agreeing any language on fossil fuels. Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho said in August 2026 that “we should abolish counterproductive Net Zero legislation pushing us towards more expensive electricity.”

This is not climate denial. The UK Conservatives’ Cheap Power plan of new gas and nuclear would, the party says, leave the electricity system “nearly 80% clean,” and Australia’s Liberals say they will still cut emissions in five-year blocks in line with comparable countries. Investment follows cheap energy and clear market rules, not targets. The 2022 and 2026 price shocks hit the UK hard partly because it had shut domestic production and firm capacity, so more domestic gas and nuclear, not faster electrification, is the security answer. To those who would ease the mandates, keeping a target you plan to miss is the worst of both worlds; to those who back technology over deadlines, we agree on cost and see no reason to keep the legal deadline at all.
positions.proponents: Conservative Party (UK); Claire Coutinho; Reform UK; Liberal Party of Australia; Net Zero Watch; Trump administration

positions.name: Reach net zero well before 2050
positions.steelman: The countries that used most of the atmosphere have the most money and technology to stop; a fair share means net zero around 2035 to 2040, not 2050.
positions.detail:
The remaining 1.5 °C budget is less than four years of current emissions, and a fair division of what is left gives rich economies little or none of it. That means net zero around 2035 to 2040, with finance for poorer countries on top. Kevin Anderson, John Broderick and Isak Stoddard concluded in 2020 that “double-digit annual mitigation rates are required of developed countries, from 2020,” and Climate Action Network Europe has called anything less than EU net zero by 2040 a lack of global leadership. Finland has already legislated carbon neutrality by 2035, proof that earlier dates are possible in a rich democracy. Clean technology is cheap enough: a 2022 study by Way and colleagues in Joule found a rapid transition likely to save trillions of dollars compared with staying on fossil fuels, before counting climate damage. Every five years of delay locks in about another 0.1 °C of warming, borne mostly by people who did least to cause it.

We are told that cuts of 10 percent a year have only ever come with economic collapse. The right comparison is mobilization, not recession: postwar reconstruction and the wartime retooling of industry show what rich economies can do when they decide to. Costs fall with speed, because learning curves reward deployment, while the cost of delay rises. Consent is lost when the burden falls on the poor; a fast transition built on public investment, frequent-flyer levies and support for low-income households can keep it. Net zero in 2050 is the global average date, and matching the average is not leadership.
positions.proponents: Climate Action Network Europe; Kevin Anderson; Government of Finland; Friends of the Earth; Greenpeace

positions.name: Pace cuts to cheap clean technology, not deadlines
positions.steelman: Pace is not a dial governments set by law; emissions fall as fast as clean options become cheaper than fossil ones, so drive down the cost instead of fixing dates.
positions.detail:
The deepest real cuts have come from cheap gas displacing coal and from cheap solar and wind, not from deadlines. Targets set far ahead of the technology produce mandates people resent, costs they notice and a backlash that endangers the whole effort, as the swings in rich-country climate law since 2023 show. In the words of the Breakthrough Institute’s Ted Nordhaus, “The long-term trajectory of decarbonization has not changed much over the last 50 years.” The useful questions are where the green premium is still high, in steel, cement, aviation, heat and firm power, and how to drive it to zero through research, demonstration, nuclear, permitting reform and early markets. Bill Gates argued in 2025 that a doomsday outlook had led the climate community to focus too much on near-term emissions goals, at the expense of the most effective work. The cost curves are our evidence: utility-scale battery storage is about 95 percent cheaper than in 2010. Make clean energy cheap and the whole world adopts it; keep it expensive and no target will hold.

Deployment does drive learning, which is why we back early markets, procurement and standards where they make technologies cheaper; we oppose economy-wide deadlines that force adoption before the technology is ready. To those who would hold the course, the dates are now a political liability that cheap technology would make unnecessary; to those who would repeal, abandoning decarbonization policy forfeits the innovation that makes energy cheap; to those who want faster cuts, the countries whose emissions are rising will adopt clean technology only when it is cheaper, and rich-country deadlines do nothing to make it so.
positions.proponents: Breakthrough Institute; Ted Nordhaus; Bill Gates; Tony Blair Institute; Bjørn Lomborg; Copenhagen Consensus Center

crux.lead: Is cutting faster in rich economies worth what it costs, once its effect on everyone else is counted?
crux.subtitle: Every camp here expects rich-country emissions to keep falling. They part over whether the next tonne cut in a wealthy country this decade buys enough avoided damage, and enough change in what other countries do, to justify its price.
crux.empirical: Part of this can be measured: how much harm each extra tonne of CO2 does, how steeply costs rise when the timetable is squeezed, including grid and backup costs that headline power prices leave out, whether rich-country deployment still makes clean technology cheaper for everyone, how much industry moves abroad when rich countries cut faster, and whether electrification softens or worsens price shocks.
crux.values: Even with every number agreed, people would still differ over how much to weigh people living in 2070 or 2100 against households paying bills today, whether past emissions oblige rich countries to move first, how much to pay to avoid a small chance of severe and irreversible warming, and how much present cost and political consent are worth spending to reduce it.
